paper_design_summary: Twenty novice designers were randomly assigned to ChatGPT, Midjourney, both tools, or no generative AI, and each completed baby-chair and tangible-music-brick conceptual design tasks (pp. 5-6, Sections 3.1-3.2). Five professional designers assessed the forty final design solutions for novelty, feasibility, usability, functional diversity and cost, with overall design-performance scores also reported (p. 7, Section 3.3.2; p. 11, Table 3). The paper does not specify whether its statistical analyses use individual ratings or scores aggregated by design or participant, so the outcome analysis unit is left null.

studies.label: Conceptual design experiment: baby chair and tangible music bricks

assignment.what_was_assigned: Participants were assigned to use ChatGPT, Midjourney, both tools, or no generative AI for both design tasks.
assignment.quote: Participants were randomly divided into four groups, which are ChatGPT Group, Midjourney Group, Combined Group, and Human Group.
assignment.locator: p. 5, Section 3.2 (Procedure); pp. 5-6 describe the training session and timed experimental tasks.

arms.name: ChatGPT Group
arms.description: Required to use ChatGPT for both design tasks (p. 6, Section 3.2). Per-arm assignment and outcome-analysis totals are not explicitly reported and are left null.

arms.name: Midjourney Group
arms.description: Required to use Midjourney for both design tasks (p. 6, Section 3.2). Per-arm assignment and outcome-analysis totals are not explicitly reported and are left null.

arms.name: Combined Group
arms.description: Required to use both ChatGPT and Midjourney for both design tasks, with the order of tool use freely chosen (pp. 5-6, Section 3.2). Per-arm assignment and outcome-analysis totals are not explicitly reported and are left null.

arms.name: Human Group
arms.description: Completed both design tasks independently without generative AI (p. 6, Section 3.2). Per-arm assignment and outcome-analysis totals are not explicitly reported and are left null.

participants.who: Novice designers recruited through a university social networking site, with less than four years of design learning experience and prior experience with both ChatGPT and Midjourney; there were no restrictions on major background. Student or professional status is not explicitly stated, so population is left null.
participants.quote: After the screening process, a total of twenty participants (thirteen females, seven males, aged 18-26, SD=2.7) who met these criteria were selected.
participants.locator: p. 5, Sections 3.1-3.2 (sample and random allocation); p. 7, Section 3.3.2 (forty final design solutions evaluated); p. 16, Section 6 (experiment involving 20 novice designers). No separate post-exclusion total is stated.

ai_tool.how_used: ChatGPT supplied text through participant prompts; Midjourney generated images from text prompts. Separate arms used each tool or both tools during conceptual design, and the Combined Group could choose their order of use (p. 4, Sections 2.2 and 3; pp. 5-6, Section 3.2).

task.description: Design a baby chair and tangible music bricks. Each participant produced an image illustrating each product design, accompanied by essential text descriptions (pp. 5-6, Section 3.2).

outcomes.name: Feasibility of final design solutions (expert ratings)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Feasibility assesses whether the design can realistically be implemented. Five professional designers rated the forty final design solutions on a 7-point scale (p. 7, Section 3.3.2); Table 3 combines both design tasks (p. 11). AI availability refers to the AI-assisted arms, whose scored designs were produced during the experimental session (pp. 5-6, Section 3.2). The statistical analysis unit and rating aggregation are not specified. Contrast directions describe the raw mean scores, not statistical significance; the four-group omnibus p-values are not pairwise tests.

outcomes.name: Cost of final design solutions (expert ratings; higher is worse)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Cost assesses the expenses of manufacturing, distributing, and maintaining a product over its lifespan. Higher scores mean poorer performance (pp. 7-8, Section 3.3.2). A treatment_higher direction therefore denotes worse cost performance, not a benefit. Five professional designers rated the forty final design solutions on a 7-point scale (p. 7, Section 3.3.2); Table 3 combines both design tasks (p. 11). AI availability refers to the AI-assisted arms, whose scored designs were produced during the experimental session (pp. 5-6, Section 3.2). The statistical analysis unit and rating aggregation are not specified. Contrast directions describe the raw mean scores, not statistical significance; the four-group omnibus p-values are not pairwise tests.

eligibility.reason: Random assignment to generative-AI assistance is explicit (p. 5, Section 3.2), and expert ratings assess participants' actual design outputs (p. 7, Section 3.3.2; p. 11, Table 3). Twenty participants were selected and then randomly allocated (p. 5, Sections 3.1-3.2; p. 16, Section 6). A separate analyzed-person denominator is not explicitly reported, so participants.n_analyzed is null; even the entire randomized sample falls below the 50-person minimum. The forty designs and five expert assessors are not additional randomized participants (p. 7, Section 3.3.2). This small randomized experiment belongs in the screening report and does not enter the core dataset or an observational context category.

one_line_finding: In the experiment with 20 randomly assigned novice designers (p. 5, Sections 3.1-3.2), Midjourney assistance yielded higher expert-rated novelty (4.60 vs 3.20; p < 0.01) and overall design performance (4.34 vs 3.59; p = 0.01) than no AI (pp. 10-11, Section 4.2 and Table 3).
